utterances.text: Your Honour, at B-50 in the schedules there's a "Selimovic" referred to. The witness has mentioned "Selinovic." It may or may not be the same person, but I just point that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also mentioned a person with the surname Cedic be taken out towards the administration building. And do you know the person's first name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: I don't know the first name, but his nickname was Ekinda.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that you saw a Zaim Cedic in your room with injuries that he received. Is that Zaim Cedic, is that the same person as Ekinda, or is it different?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: No, it's a totally different person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Zaim Cedic still at the KP Dom when you left, do you know?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Yes, he remained there after me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also you mentioned a Mr. Mandzo and Hasan Dzano or Hasan Dzanko who you saw their injuries in your room. Were they still there when you left the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Yes, they remained there after me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the break, you stated that when Nurko Nisic was taken towards the administration building, shortly after you heard the sound of him screaming and you believed he was being beaten at that stage, and you also said that you heard Halim Konjo's voice as he was being beaten after he was taken to the administration building. Of any of the other people that you saw taken out, did you hear any of them particularly screaming or shouting?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: You mean was I able to recognise their voices? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember the last individual we mentioned, Cedic, known as Ekinda, I recognised his voice when he was beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that these 25 or 26 people were taken out over a two- to three-week period in June. You stated that they were taken out in groups of three or four, and you've stated they were taken out at about dusk. Of the people, the other people that were taken out, of the names that you have mentioned, you didn't particularly hear their voices as they were being beaten, did you hear anything, after these other people were taken out, coming from the administration building?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Well, I heard voices, but only -- I only recognised the voices of these three persons. I told you it was in the evening hours, at dusk, after dinner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the other occasions, the occasions when you couldn't recognise the voices, what did you hear?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: I heard screaming and moaning, just like with all others that were beaten up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did this happen after every group was taken out into the administration building, or just some of them or most of them? Can you say?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: There would always be screaming and moaning. That would follow -- that would come after each group entered the administrative building. I don't know if all of them were beaten, only some of them were beaten. I couldn't see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the atmosphere, the atmosphere like at the KP Dom whilst these beatings were going on? How did you feel?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: I was in a state of shock. The fear was among the inmates. None of us could talk about it. We all felt lost. I don't know how to describe this feeling to you. It was simply a great shock to us. We never knew who would be the next one to be taken out, whether it would be me or somebody else, so it was a time of waiting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you or anyone you know of make complaints to the guards as to what was going on at this time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: I personally didn't, and I doubt that anybody else did because we were not allowed to talk to the guards. It was forbidden to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst you were at the KP Dom, did you know who the warden was?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: I heard from other inmates that it was Krnojelac, Milorad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Milorad Krnojelac from before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Yes. He was my math teacher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him in the KP Dom whilst you were detained?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: I never saw him, not once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you heard from other detainees that he was the warden. Do you remember any specific name of a detainee that told you this?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: I can't remember, but we would normally hear it when we talked amongst ourselves. There were a lot of inmates there, so I can't really remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you were arrested and taken to the KP Dom on the 26th of May, did you know who the warden of the KP Dom was?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness stated that he heard from other inmates that Milorad Krnojelac was the warden, and there is no way he could have seen other inmates before he came to KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But the answer which he gave doesn't limit that to his knowledge. He says he was told by the other detainees. He's now being asked did he have any knowledge of that before he went into the KP Dom. I would think the answer is probably as you suggested, but it doesn't stop the Prosecution from asking it. You go ahead, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know who the warden was of the KP Dom before you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: I wasn't sure of it. There were stories, rumours in town, but the first official information I received was the one I received at the KP Dom, from inmates. Because there were stories circulating the town, indicating that he was the warden even prior to me going to KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did you hear these stories from?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: When I talked to my wife, she told me. I don't know who she heard it from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who the supervisor of the guards was whilst you were at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Mitar Rasevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know him from before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him whilst you were at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About on how many occasions did you see him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: I saw him for the first time when I was in the isolation cell. The door was open that morning and he was standing at the door, and that was the first time I saw him. And then afterwards I would see him, I don't know how many times, but I would normally see him as he was passing through the compound of KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the morning that you saw him, the morning that you saw him when you were in the isolation cell, was that when you were put in the isolation cell or was it the day later, when you left the isolation cell?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: That was on the following day, when I left the isolation cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he say anything to you on that day?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: He asked me why I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you tell him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: I said, "Well, why do you ask me? I don't know," because I myself don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was -- what would Mitar Rasevic wear when you saw him at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Like all other guards, he had a blue uniform on him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whilst you were at the KP Dom, did you know a Savo Todovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: I can't remember right now. The name sounds familiar, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told the Court that you were released from the KP Dom on the 7th of July, 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You arrived at the KP Dom: Halim Dedovic, Hajro Sabanovic, and your uncle. Do you know what happened to each of them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Hajro and Halim never returned, as far as I know, and my uncle was released that same year. I'm not sure which month it was, whether it was August or September. I'm not quite sure. But it was that same year, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Halim and Hajro never returned. Were they still in the KP Dom when you were released?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Yes. They remained there after me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst you were at the KP Dom, were you ever told by anyone in authority why you were being detained there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever advised of your right of having your detention reviewed?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: I was never told this by anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whilst you were at the KP Dom, were you ever charged with any offence?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: I didn't discuss it with anybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you explain the circumstances of your release? How were you released?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: On that 7th of July of 1992, sometime in the morning, a guard came and called out my name. I went out with him and we went to the entrance, into the administrative building. He told me to wait there for the papers to be ready and then he told me, "You are released. You'll go home." I waited there for some five or ten minutes. The doors opened once again, and then when I went through the hallway in that administrative building, so when I went through it and through another door, I came out and I saw my wife waiting there, and then I realised that this was really happening. Because prior to that, I simply didn't believe in what he was saying; I thought I was just being taken away like all the others were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your wife bring a document to the KP Dom to organise your release?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Yes. She managed to obtain a document through some friends, this releasing document, and I was released based on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she tell you who she obtained the document from?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: This document was signed by Dr. Mandic, and it had three more signatures there by Koprivica, Starovic, and a third one was something starting with a "V." I believe it was Vladicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could ask the usher to show the witness P418.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is it necessary? It's in evidence already. He doesn't have to identify it. I'm just trying to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps just in relation to the signatures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: We have a copy here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that the signature of Dr. Mandic was on this document. Where does that signature appear? On the left-hand side or the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: It's on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen Dr. Mandic's signature before or have you been told that that's his signature?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: I was told this. I never saw his signature prior to this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who told you that was his signature on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Well, his signature is there, and when I came out and talked to my wife, she explained to me how it came that I was released and who had to sign the document for me to be released, and that was him; he was that person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did she also explain to you that the other three that you've mentioned that signed the document were the ones that signed the document? Did she tell you that or did you find that out some other way?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: She told me that, because she was well informed about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know who Dr. Mandic was at that time, what position he held?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Well, in further conversations with my wife, she told me that he was a member of the SDS Crisis Staff and, based on what she knew, he was the person in charge, the person who decided on life or death of inmates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that document it states that you had an obligation to report to the police station in the Serb municipality of Foca. When you left, did you report to the police station daily?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: No, because as soon as I was released, we left Foca; we went away. We didn't dare remain there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Cross-examined by Mr. Bakrac:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. I'm Mihajlo Bakrac and I'm one of the counsel for the accused Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should first like to ask you to pause a little after you hear my question, before you answer, in order to make the job of the interpreters slightly easier and to avoid overlapping the questions and answers. You just replied when asked by my learned friend -- or rather, you said sometime this morning that before your arrest, that is, between the outbreak of the armed conflict and the arrest, you, to all intents and purposes, spent all that time in the house, that is, inside, either in the house or in the cellar. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who else was with you there? Your wife and who else?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: I don't know which place you have in mind because during those several days we moved from -- to about two or three different places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were other Muslims with you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: In my house, while we were in my house, there were, yes, Muslims. At the time when we were in my mother-in-law's cellar, there were Muslims, too. When we were in the cellar of my relative, there were also -- there were both Muslims and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they also staying in the cellar or moving about the town?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: At that time, during the shelling, they were in the cellar with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when the shelling stopped, if I understood you well, you and your wife went back to a flat and did not leave it until the military police came after you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: I stayed in that building, in my relative's flat, for a few days more, and then when the shelling stopped, I went back home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then tell us, how is it possible that you knew the rumours that went around the town? You first said that you heard from other detainees who was the warden, and when asked again by the Prosecutor, you then said that you may have heard stories which circulated the town. So how could you hear those stories which went around the town if you were inside all the time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Well, when we went back to -- went back home, then my wife would go out now and then to get some supplies or get whatever we needed, and she would then drop by her mother or by this relative again, and there were always rumours which spread among people. Some bit of news would always leak from somewhere; I don't know from where.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did her mother dare go out? You say she went to visit her mother, but did she dare go out? Because you told us Muslims were prohibited from going out.

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Yes. It was prohibited, but at great peril to herself she nevertheless had to go out from time to time. Her mother did not go around the town because we were afraid because she was in poor health.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then, how could she hear the rumours around the town?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: I don't know who she learned it from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that in your statement to the OTP investigators, you said that before the armed conflict, the SDA had already taken over the executive post in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: In that statement, I did say "take over," but I did not mean all the executive posts because, before the democratic elections, most of the executive posts were in the hands of people of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't really understand what you said. Is it correct that you said that the SDA had taken over the executive posts in the town? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Yes, but you did not let me finish. I did say that, but I did not mean that they had taken over literally all the executive posts in the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then did you mean that they had taken over the majority of executive posts in the town?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Yes. By that, I meant that they had taken over a large number of executive posts because, owing to the votes they got in the elections, they became entitled to a larger number of executive posts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also correct that you told the OTP investigators that following the elections in 1991, ethnic intolerance began to emerge, to be felt?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it also true that you told the OTP investigators that there were Muslim military units in Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I shall then read out to you only one sentence from the statement that you made, if that is correct, and I see that the Prosecutor also refers to it, on the 2nd of December, 1998. Did you give a statement to the OTP on that date?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "In Foca there were some Muslim armed units, but without strict, rigid, formal organisation. I did not try to organise anything or defend Foca."

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, those were groups of men who were not organised in any significant military formations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that in that same statement, right after this, you said that, "Dedovic had told the military police, when pressured, that I was a member of the SDA and commander of Muslim armed units"?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke about the day when you arrived in the KP Dom, or rather, the evening when you got there, and you said that the military police interrogated you. I would merely like to clarify whether it was the night between the 24th and 25th of May or between the 25th and the 26th of May.

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: They brought me that evening, so it was the 24th, and it was that night, between the 24th and the 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the next night, between the 25th and the 26th of May, you spent in the isolation cell, is it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: In the isolation cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that on that occasion when you were brought there and when you were interrogated, that at that time there was no electricity in the KP Dom. Was it a frequent occurrence for the KP Dom, I mean, to be without lights?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: When I was there during I don't know how many days, there was no electricity at all, at least, in our dormitories. As far as I can remember, down there -- well, I don't know that, but be that as it may, in our dormitories, we never had any lights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what you told us about, told us that happened, happened in the administrative building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This place where you were interrogated, that is, the administrative building, and it is without electricity, too, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: When I was brought there, that night there was no electricity. It was dark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was there any electricity, any lights in the compound?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. After that interrogation, were you ever beaten again or struck again or mistreated in any way during your stay in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: You mean after that first night?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you told the OTP investigators that, during your detention, there were 500 detainees in the KP Dom altogether?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: According to my calculations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also say that a doctor called Cedo Dragovic regularly paid visits to the prison, and you also added that he never treated beaten prisoners, he also administered medicines to those with heart conditions?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Yes, Cedo would come and give medicines to heart patients, but those who had sustained injuries during beatings, he never extended any medical aid to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I shall now ask you with reference to persons we mentioned and about whom you told us they were taken away and never returned, and I shall ask you to tell me to the best of your recollection what rooms were they taken from and, if you can remember, the dates. Halim Konjo.

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Halim Konjo, I don't know the number of the room in that building, but if I had a drawing, then I could show you which room he was in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it will suffice if you tell us, since you don't know the number of the room, whether it was in the left or right wing of the building.

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Halim Konjo was in the left wing of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the date when he was taken out, if you can remember it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: I don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Emir Frasto, which room was he in, and do you know the date when he was taken away?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: He was also in the left wing of the building. I don't remember the dates of any of those departures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Munib Veiz, what room was he taken from?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: He was also in the left wing of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you don't know the number of the room, do you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the second Veiz whose first name you can't remember, what room was he taken from?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: He was also in the left wing of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you don't know the date?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: I can't give you any date, because I simply do not remember any of the dates when they were taken away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Kemal Isanovic, which room was he taken out from?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: The left part of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nurko Nisic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Left wing of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mehmed Pasalic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Left wing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Kruno Marinovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Left wing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Matovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Likewise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean the left wing of the building?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Husein Rikalo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Left wing of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Kemo Dzelilovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Left wing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Selimovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: He also came from the left wing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Cedic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Cedic was also from the left wing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you told OTP investigators in your statement of 3rd and 4th May, 1995 that: "We could see who was coming in and out of the administrative building but we could not see what was going on inside since the windows of the administrative building were opaque"?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you also say in your statement to the OTP the following: "The windows on the front side, which faced the administrative building, the windows of the prisoners' quarters, had window panes painted over so we could not see them"?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: No, we could not see them because they were painted over, but there were other windows on the right-hand side of the room through which one could also see the door leading to the administrative building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But here you said that the window panes were painted over and that you could not see anything through them. You did not explain that there were some other windows through which you could see.

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: The windows on that lower part of the building were painted; and the windows on the right-hand side of the dormitory, of the rooms, were not painted, and through them one could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really avoided showing any ground plans, but perhaps it would be useful if the witness told us which windows he has in mind, that is, which windows he says were transparent. To speed matters up, I will give him our copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Which -- have you got the six --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the same copy that Mr. Smith used to show it. I don't know simply if it is marked -- yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: To assist the transcript, I think I breached my own injunction and spoke over Mr. Bakrac, but I referred to Exhibit 88.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please show us, then, those right-hand windows.

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Here, on this side of the building, which could not be drawn here. So there, on this side of the building. If you stand here, then they're on the left-hand side, but if you look from the building, then it's on the right-hand side. So these windows overlook this part here. What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The prisoners' quarters. You told us that the windows across the administrative building were opaque, but from these windows, those windows which faced the building on the left-hand side were transparent and we could see through them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is showing -- the witness is pointing at, if I may call it that, annex B of the prisoners' quarters, the windows which cannot be seen on this drawing and which overlook annex A and the left part of the building. He also pointed at the -- he also said that the windows in annex A which face the administrative building had been painted over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please now show, if we are in front of annex A and look at the right-hand windows and the right wing of the building, were those windows painted over too?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question? Where? If I stand where?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you stand in front of the prison itself.

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: You mean here?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. A little bit to the right. So to the right of this annex. You now showed us the left one, which overlooks A, but I mean the right wing, which overlooks the furniture factory.

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: So you mean if I stand here, is it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Windows which overlook the furniture factory. You know the furniture factory is number 7.

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So windows overlooking that, were those windows painted over?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the windows next to the right-hand entrance into the building, into the prison, painted over?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: You mean these windows here? Yes, these were small windows, windows where isolation cells were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the windows to the left?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: The windows to the left were the windows of the passage which was in the part with the lavatories, with toilets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And windows on the upper floor?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Windows on the upper floor I don't remember because I never stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We don't need the sketch anymore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you told the OTP investigators in your statement of the 2nd of December, 1998, that is, in your latter statement, that you said that, during your detention, a man in a camouflage olive-green/grey colour entered the room in which you were kept?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that you told OTP investigators that you never heard any shots, only blows and screams?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the names of three men who signed, in addition to Dr. Mandic, your discharge, your release document. And in the statement that you made to the OTP, to which you referred just now, you said that the release certificate was signed by Dr. Mandic and three other persons from the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So why didn't you say then that it was those three persons, since today you told us that you had been told that by your wife after you left?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. Could you repeat it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you say the OTP investigators in 1998, which were those three names? Why did you say only three more persons from the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose because they never asked me who it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me only if you stated that the military police was under the command of the military authorities. Did you say that to OTP investigators?

utterances.speaker: FWS-3 [Name redacted]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Re-examination, Mr. Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You may now leave. Thank you for giving evidence. Wait till the blinds have been lowered on that side of the courtroom so that you may leave without the public being able to identify you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would have to address a very urgent procedural matter that just raised today right now. We received a message in relation to the Witness 49 who is going to testify, who was supposed to be going to testify through videolink conference next Tuesday, and we just received the message that this person, because of his poor health, is now in hospital and underwent operation two days ago, and he is not able to come and testify on the date we had thought he would. And we have contacted the son of this witness, and he said his father is -- has to stay in the hospital for some more time, and he thinks it would be probably two weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: How would that affect the prospect of the Prosecution case finishing before he's available?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When it is actually two weeks only, then we do not have a problem at all; but if it is not possible and the health conditions are so bad, we consider then to simply strike him from the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You realise, of course, that to fix another date, there is a certain leadup time required. I gather on this particular occasion, because fair warning had been given in advance, it took less time to arrange than it usually does. So you'd better be in touch with the registry about it. The moment you believe that there is another date that he will be available, you should notify the registry to start making arrangements, even before coming to the Trial Chamber to get another order. Now, you can lift the blinds, thanks. We're going to deal with a procedural matter. Is that all you want to say about that particular matter?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We will cancel the order that the videolink be heard on Tuesday, and we're very grateful to the people who arranged it for doing so, even though they'll probably be very unhappy to hear that their efforts have been wasted. Now, about the application by the Defence for psychological examination of the accused, we've read all of the documents. This is yours, is it, Ms. Kuo?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what the Prosecution is attempting to say in paragraph 4 of its further response. We had invited you to ask for your own expert to be appointed, and obviously that will be granted; but you then go on to say that you are going to wait until the registry appoints its expert as it is possible that the Prosecution will agree to the registrar's expert without need to engage the services of a third psychologist. I think that there is no need to have three psychologists.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We spoke with the representative in the registrar's office to find out who, who among the sort of certified doctors would be available to be appointed, and we were informed that we would have no choice, that it was not up to the Prosecution to decide, that the registrar would simply appoint someone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think you'd better tell the registry that they'll do what we say, and if we say the Prosecution may choose one, they will be entitled to choose one. And it's quite absurd for anybody down there to suggest otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I can certainly convey that, Your Honour, but this is simply what we were told. And in light of, what we thought would be the wisest thing, because we also think three is probably too much, is to wait to see whom the registrar on their own choice, and if we thought that was an appropriate person, then we would simply not ask for another person. Now, if the Court wishes us, then, to tell the registrar that we would simply in the first instance choose, we're certainly happy to do that, it's just that we were told by the registrar we were not really in a position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, you can tell whoever it was down in the registrar's that if they have some problems with what we're proposing, they can come and talk to us. It is far simpler in anything like this for there to be an expert appointed on either side who are both present, who can have competing views, perhaps, which will then be presented to the Court if the material becomes relevant. But the idea of a Court-appointed expert is appropriate in some cases, but we do not ourselves see that it is appropriate in this case. I think the registry, whoever it is down there, may have misunderstood the situation, to give them the benefit of the doubt, but I do sometimes wonder who they think are running these trials. Well, now, if we then give you the right to choose an expert, then you will choose somebody perhaps from the list, or do you want somebody else who also speaks the language and comes from the former Yugoslavia to be able to be in the same position as the expert recommended or sought by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Our reading of the rule is that we are required --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, look, your concern for the sanctity of Rule 74 bis is very commendable, but it's clear that it has not always been followed in the past. It has not been even followed by this Chamber in the past. It may be that the list needs to be brought up to date, but we're not going to allow a very technical problem to do with a Rule to stand in the way with getting on with this trial. And we believe that it is appropriate that the, that the examination be carried out by a person who does understand the language and the background of the former Yugoslavia. If this becomes an issue in the case, such an expert would obviously be the best to assist us. So if the Defence -- I'm sorry, if the Prosecution seeks a similar expert, then we would grant it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. What we'll do, then, is look at the lists that the registrar has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: -- and then supplement it, perhaps, and suggest someone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Right. Well, is there anything that you want to add Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do you want to add anything to that, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I am not a psychologist, I'm a lawyer, but I did look into this aspect, and I have talked to experts and psychologists. The core of our proposal is to obtain an adequate and valid and fair result. I was always being told that a presence of a third person, be it an interpreter, a Defence counsel, anybody else, does not allow for the possibility of a comprehensive and valid expert opinion. We were also told --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I don't want to stop you, but I said is there anything further you want to add? We've read your submissions, and you've said all of this in your submissions, and we believe that it's appropriate in this case. So unless you want to talk yourself out of it, I suggest you pass on to something that's not in your written submissions if you want to add anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honours, I think that this new situation which was created by the answer given to the Prosecution creates -- brings us to a situation where we will have a third person while the tests are being conducted. We did indicate that these tests are standardised. There is perhaps a possibility that I miscomprehended something, but what we understood is that our expert who carries out the testing will present all of the results of the testing and results of his discussions with the accused, and this will be an expert from the list of the Prosecution or the registrar's. But it was our understanding that there would also be a third person, which means another expert, which would also be present and participate in this testing, and this is why I wanted to explain that the presence of a third person, whoever it may be, will inhibit to some degree the accused, and the contact between a psychologist and the subject that was tested will not be appropriate. So this is what the Defence believes. We believe this is a new detail, and we wanted to bring this to your attention. We are prepared to present the results of the expert opinion to any other expert who will look it over; however, we do not agree with the other expert being present during the examination for the very reasons that I have just stated to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, the third person you're talking about is a second expert, so there will be the accused and the two experts. Is that what you're worried about?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. Not because we have any bad intentions - I don't think that I even need to dispute this - but simply saying a third person, a third party, and I'm bringing this to your attention from the view of the accused, could bring to -- certain inhibition to the accused, to influence him to not be as open and as cooperative. So this presence of a third person, whether it is an interpreter, a counsel, or an expert from another country, or a person who is sent by the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I have been practising in the law for the unfortunately long period now 42 years. Throughout that period, I have a lot to do with cases involving medical examinations. Now, I am sure that it's no different if we have somebody such as a Yugoslav in my country, where there are many of them, being examined by a doctor there or being examined by a doctor here in the Netherlands. It's almost invariable that both sides have their own expert there during the course of that examination; otherwise, it would be productive of possible mischief, but it is also something which usually assists the party who is calling a doctor to give evidence about the results of that examination, whoever that doctor may be, the fact that both doctors have seen the same thing, heard the same results, seen the same tests being conducted. It is invariably so. I can understand your concern that there would be an interpreter there which rather suggests that the Prosecution would be even better advised to have somebody similar to your expert who speaks the language, but it would be inappropriate for this to be done without somebody from the Prosecution there as well; otherwise, there will be all sorts of suggestions which will be available to be made which could not otherwise be made if both experts are there at the same time. Now, I do not understand why your client would feel any more diffident in speaking to an expert -- to one expert from his own country or two experts from his own country. You don't suggest, do you, that there's some special relationship between him and Ms. Najman?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. In fact, they never met before; there is no relationship there. I'm simply concerned, and I have already stated to you I'm not a psychologist, I'm a lawyer, however I heard from psychologists that they are standardised tests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, of course there are standardised tests, but if I may say so, you're destroying the value of any expert opinion you have unless there is an expert from the other side there. That's the point I'm trying to make. And there cannot be any diffidence on your client's part in talking to two experts, particularly if they're from Yugoslavia, together.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, then. We misunderstood each other. You are now mentioning two experts from Yugoslavia who speak the same language and who are from the same area, so my apologies, Your Honours. If the Prosecution has an expert with these qualifications, or perhaps the registry, if they should appoint such an expert, then, of course, it is a different matter. In that case, we will not be needing an interpreter, and I think that two experts will be able to conduct this task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Kuo, that only underlines what I said before: If you're going to get any value of having an expert there, it would be preferable, would it not, to have one from Yugoslavia and who speaks the language?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And we'll attempt to find someone, given the practical constraints.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh, yes, of course, we understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: By motion filed by the Defence on the 5th of June, the Defence seeks to have the registry appoint Ms. Ana Najman, N-a-j-m-a-n, of Belgrade to perform a psychological examination of the accused, such examination to include certain specified tests which are said to be standardised for the South Slavic population. Ms. Najman has been nominated by the Defence because of what is said to be a need for the examination to be conducted by someone from the same linguistic region who also knows the ethnological, cultural, and anthropological region of the environment as the accused, a factor said to be a very important segment of "psychodiagnostics." Objection was taken by the Prosecution in its response filed on the 8th of January upon two bases: first, that no ground had been stated which was relevant to any of the issues so far raised by the Defence; and secondly, that Ms. Najman was not one of the experts named in the list drawn up by the registrar in accordance with Rule 74 bis of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence. On the 9th of January, the Trial Chamber directed the accused to identify the precise issue to which the psychological examination would be relevant in the absence of any relevant issue raised by him in the Defence Pre-Trial brief. Counsel for the accused then identified, in a document dated the 12th of January, the purpose of the proposed examination as being "to establish the personality structure of the accused in order to help clarify his conduct in the situations of receiving orders, their understanding and execution within the professional tasks he was assigned as head of a part of the prison, as well as of other requirements asked from him in the war circumstances." Counsel for both parties then had a helpful discussion in which it was made plain that the Defence seeks to ascertain whether there is, in fact, any psychological basis for the actions of the accused. If such a basis is discovered, then the Defence will no doubt consider whether to amend its Pre-Trial brief to include it as an issue in the case. The Prosecution has now filed a further response, dated the 17th of January, in which it states that, subject to argument as to the relevance and admissibility of the findings obtained in this examination, it has no objection to such an examination being ordered. In those circumstances, it is unnecessary for this Trial Chamber to determine whether an order should be made to support what is quite frankly, on its face, a fishing expedition. If it did have to determine that issue, it would have to consider a number of matters, including the fact that the accused is in custody and is unable to arrange such an examination himself. The Prosecution does, however, maintain its objection to Ms. Najman upon the basis that she is not on the registry list kept in accordance with the Rule, but the Prosecution also realistically acknowledges that there is no expert on that list who speaks B/C/S and who is from the former Yugoslavia. The Trial Chamber is satisfied that in the particular circumstances of this case, it is reasonable that the examination should be performed by such an expert. Ms. Najman has already been accepted as an expert witness in two other cases before the Tribunal, having been appointed as such by the registar. Those are the cases of Dokmanovic and of Radic. It may be that the list drawn up in accordance with the Rule is ripe for being brought up-to-date, and the Trial Chamber will draw the registrar's attention to the need for it to be brought up-to-date. However, the Trial Chamber does not accept that Rule 74 bis should, in all justice, stand in the way of this application, which the Trial Chamber grants. In accordance with the Trial Chamber's invitation to do so, the Prosecution has sought the appointment also of a medical expert of its own choosing to be present at and to participate in the examination to be conducted by Ms. Najman. This was objected to by the Defence upon the basis that it would somehow affect the validity of the examination to be carried out by Ms. Najman. In my own very long experience of dealing with medical examinations related to litigation, I can only say that such an objection should be rejected. It is almost invariable that both parties should be represented at such an examination. The presence of representatives of both parties enhances the views which are formed. There can be no suggestion made of any misconduct because of the presence of both experts. The Trial Chamber does recognise the problem which may arise if the Prosecution chooses an expert who is not from Yugoslavia and does not have the background which Ms. Najman has. Because of the need for an interpreter, that certainly or may well interfere with the validity of the examination. The Prosecution accepts this and will do its best to ensure that the expert which it chooses will be from the former Yugoslavia and does speak B/C/S. Such an expert will also necessarily not be in the registrar's list, but the Trial Chamber will nevertheless grant that request as well. If there is any particular problem which the Prosecution has in obtaining another such expert, bearing in mind the situation between the Tribunal generally and the country of Serbia, the matter can be raised again before the Trial Chamber. An order will be drawn up and signed tomorrow. Now, is there anything further that needs to be done about that matter?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Right. Well, now we have one other witness left on the list. When I say "left on the list," we were told first of all that 47 could not come but that we may have 144 in his place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yes. He's available. He's been waiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Right. Now, does he have protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yes. The Court has granted a pseudonym and facial distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Right. Well, let's have the blinds down again while he's brought in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: While we're waiting, Your Honour, perhaps we can have the name sheet for this witness numbered as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P419 and it will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Please make the declaration in the document which is being shown to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Kuo. Examined by Ms. Kuo:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you is a piece of paper which has been entered as Exhibit P419. You'll see the letters and numbers FWS-144. Underneath that, is that your name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Underneath your name, is that your birth date?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, in April of 1992, where did you live? What town?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: In April of 1992, I lived in a village called Jelec, near Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far from Foca is Jelec?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: About 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnic composition of Jelec?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Mostly Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With whom did you live?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: With my wife and two sons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you work in Jelec?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: No. I work in a Sarajevo company, and at that time I worked on a construction site in the town of Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what kind of work you did?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: I was working as a metal worker with metal constructions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the war in Foca started, did you see villages near Jelec burning?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Yes. After the fall of Foca, the Serb forces set on fire villages -- all the villages leading up to my village of Jelec.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us the names of those villages?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Well, based on my recollection, Susjesno -- from what we could see from my village, Susjesno, Budanj, Izvisno, and Jelec was the last.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnic composition of those villages that were burned?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Bosniaks only.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the residents of Jelec do anything to try to defend themselves?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Well, for personal safety, we created guard units so that we could defend ourselves from a much more powerful SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you participate in this guard?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Yes, for personal safety of my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Not me. There were several rifles and people would pass it on as they were standing guard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when the residents of Jelec who were standing guard were asked to surrender weapons?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Yes. A representative of our village was invited to a meeting with a representative of SDS from the village of Miljevina. They gave us an ultimatum, requesting us to surrender of weapons in our possession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you surrender your weapons?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: At the time, I didn't have one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the other people in Jelec surrender their weapons?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Most of them surrendered. Perhaps those who were the bravest refused to obey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was Jelec attacked?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: 5th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in Jelec when it was attacked?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where specifically were you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Well, specifically I was with my family, at home. However, when the shelling of the village started, we fled into a nearby forest. The entire population of the village did so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people was that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Well, my village had approximately 300 households.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how many people fled into the forest with you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: The entire village had to flee, because we could not remain in the residential area due to the shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the forest, were you able to see any destruction in Jelec?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Yes. There was an elevation from which we could follow the entire course of setting on fire this village of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What specifically was set on fire?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Well, everything that stood in their way was set on fire. They didn't leave anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "they," whom do you mean?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: I meant those Serb forces. I'm not sure who they were, but based on the stories I heard, those were White Eagles from Serbia, and they were escorted by our neighbours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the forest, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: We remained in the forest for some three or four days; however, we had no more food, so we were forced to head towards Sarajevo en masse as refugees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you reach Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: No. On the road to Sarajevo, in Kalinovik we were met by Serb forces again and detained us in a gym in Kalinovik. Then interrogation ensued, questioning. After that, those who were military-able were singled out and, three or four days later, deported towards Bileca to a campsite that belonged to former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that it's 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll resume at 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m. 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Kuo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were at the gym in Kalinovik, was your family with you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Only briefly. Perhaps one night, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was your family taken, then?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: My family stayed in Kalinovik, and we who were military-able were deported to Bileca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "military-able," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: I mean all the adult men up to a certain age limit, that is, including fifties or ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you part of that group?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Yes, and my elder son.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old was your son at that time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: He was born in 1971, so that he had -- he was 20 something, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us your son's name, please?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: My son's name, I don't know if -- can it be protected?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Actually, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'll withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If you'd like to have it written down.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: It's actually not necessary at this point. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many men were taken to Bileca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: About 50 neighbours of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were all of these people from Jelec?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Absolutely, all were from Jelec and nowhere else, only Jelec.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you kept at Bileca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: We stayed 25 days in Bileca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were taken to Bileca, were there other people there as well?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Yes. There were also men from the Dubrovnik front of Croat origin, but they were not in the same cells with us. They were in adjoining cells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what shape those people were in?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Very bad because they had gone through horrible torture, whereas we were not tortured at all, except some minor provocations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you -- when were you taken from Bileca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: From Bileca I was taken away, well, shortly before the 1st of June because I know that on the 1st of June I was returned to the KP Dom in Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "returned," what do you mean? Were you there already, or you were taken there for the first time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: I was returned to Kalinovik from which I went to Bileca, and from Kalinovik to the camp in Foca for the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was taken with you to KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: All of us who had gone to Bileca, we all, down to the last one, came back to Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the Croats who were at Bileca taken with you to KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: No. They stayed behind in Bileca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were taken to the KP Dom, what room were you placed in?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was a room on the uppermost floor, and I think it was Room 22. I am sure that it was the top floor of one of the pavilions, and I think it was the fourth floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were the other men from Jelec taken?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: All those who were returned from Bileca -- do you mean the men coming back from Bileca?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: They were all put in the same room, that room, 22.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there men in Room 22 who were not from Jelec?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: At the time when we were brought there, there was nobody else; but after that, in the course of the day, they filled rooms with men who were not from Jelec.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were those other men from?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: I didn't really know them, but as they came one by one, they began talking to us, and I know that, for instance, a group was brought from Tjentiste.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you kept in Room 22?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: I couldn't really remember the date. In Room 22 I may have stayed until the end of 1992, even though that is not official because I can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What other rooms were you kept in during your time at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: There were some selections made of the inmates. A work group was set up and put in a room below 22, and I was moved to Room 16 later on. That was on the ground floor of that same pavilion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you kept at KP Dom, total?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: From that 1st of June, 1992, until the 10th of October, 1994, which means almost 900 days, including Bileca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were kept at KP Dom, were detainees ever beaten?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Yes, since my arrival in June. As for the worst torture and beatings, it happened mostly in those months, June, July, until September. June and July were, I should say, critical as regards those crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time of day or night did the beatings occur?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: There was a set time. It was largely in the early evening hours that guards would come in with a list, which means that somebody made the selection of those men, and they would call them out from dormitories and then taken out of the compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you able to see?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: We were not able to see anything. We could only follow them from the dormitories until they left the prison yard, the compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see where they went from the dormitory?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: From the dormitories, they would go to the main gate, to the -- where they had the control, and that was all that we could see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear anything from that point on?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Those individual cases, those men they took out, perhaps one, two, or three would happen as soon as they would go through the prison gate, that is, as soon as they would go through the gate, one could hear screams and yelling and beating immediately after that, and sometimes it took hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do when you heard the screaming?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't all that simple. We tried to flee to the corners, to the remotest corners of our room, but we could not really help not hearing it. Some tried to cover their heads with pillows, and there were also some who would lean through the windows and listen to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us how you felt when you heard this?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: I somehow managed to cope with it, because what could I do? That's the fate of the man, and I somehow summoned courage to bear it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the screaming, did you hear or see anything?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: After that ritual of beating, those screams and all the rest would die out, would die down. And then a car, which we could recognise because it had characteristic sound - I guess its exhaust pipe was missing - so we would hear this car being switched on and head for the bridge on the Drina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us where the sound of the screaming was coming from? First of all, which direction?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: I could not really give you the exact direction, but say the administrative building and then the main entrance. To my -- to what I managed to learn during my stay there, there was supposedly a cell in the administrative building where people were reportedly beaten, and allegedly there were also some links in the floor to which those men were tied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us where the sound of the car with the broken exhaust pipe was coming from?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: The sound always came from in front of the administration building when it would be switched on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know that the car went toward the bridge?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Well, it was nighttime, as a rule, especially in those first evenings, and we would peer through the window and watch. Since we were on the topmost floor, we had a rather good view over the administrative building, a good view of a bridge which was partly hidden by a tree, so that all we could see were the lights of that car, and of course its sound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see -- what about the lights? What did you see regarding the lights? Where were the lights coming from?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Lights were moving towards the bridge, and then, when presumably the vehicle would reach the bridge, they would be off and the vehicle would then continue to the end of the bridge and come back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the vehicle stop, or rather the lights of the vehicle come to a stop?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: The lights would be switched off on the bridge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to clarify this. Could you see the vehicle itself or just the lights from the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: The vehicle could not be seen at all. We could follow it by the sound it made, and it was very loud because it did not have the exhaust pipe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the lights, how do you know that the lights came from the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: It was only at that time that that vehicle with that sound moved. There were no other lights, nor did any other vehicle move about at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I'd like to have, with the assistance of the usher, the witness shown Prosecution Exhibit P18, photograph 7528.

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: This.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us in the photograph --

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Here. This.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- what you saw from Room 22?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: This building with three chimneys and the tree in front, this is the administrative building. Yes, that's right. And we could see it from my room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at where there is a yellow arrow, can you see what's there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: No, I can't really make it out. I'm not -- I can't make it out whether that is the beginning of the bridge or what. But the tree hid the bridge, looking from my window, except the end of the bridge on the opposite sides of the Drina that you could glimpse in daytime; at night it was absolutely impossible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that the tree obscured your vision of the bridge. Could you see the light of the car through the leaves of the tree?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like --

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: It was my pleasure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: -- the usher to have another exhibit shown to this Witness. It's P6/5.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you point out to us where Room 22 is?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: I can if you give me a moment. Room 22, yes, this is the room, and it was -- it had some space with lockers, and the lavatory, living-room, and four dormitories, and of those four, I was in the front one, in this one here on the last floor, Room 22.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Let the record reflect that the witness has pointed to one of the bedrooms in Room 22, to the -- the one to the right, closest to the administrative building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you show us the window or windows that you were looking out of when you saw the light on the bridge?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: There were windows on this side too, but also there were windows on this side, facing the administrative building. So both these dormitories had their windows overlooking the administrative building, and through those windows we could clearly see or, rather, monitor the movement of the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The windows in those two front bedrooms, could you -- which one did you look out of when you saw the headlights on the bridge? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: There were two windows in this particular room. I can't remember which one of the two. That is something that I don't remember. But we tried to peep out because we were -- it was strictly forbidden to look through the window, and we were punished by beating if they caught us.
