utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Let the record reflect that the witness pointed to the windows that would be in the bedroom which he identified as his. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know someone named Safet Avdic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Safet Avdic, I knew him before the war, and it also happened that we shared the same dormitory in Room 22 for a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he in Room 22 with you when you -- when the beatings that you described happened?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, he was. I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to identify any of the people who were taken out and beaten in this way?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: The only man I knew personally, because he had relatives in my village, was Tulek. Before the war, he worked for that same KP Dom. He was in my village, at the fish farm, at the time when the war broke out; that is, he was a guard there before the war. So that when my village was torched, he, together with the villagers of Jelec, experienced this whole calvary that we went through, to Kalinovik, to Bileca, to KP Dom, and stayed in Room 22 with us for a certain time. But shortly after that, he was called out, taken for interrogation in the administrative building. And after that first round, he returned to the room, but only briefly, only to pick up his belongings, and was then transferred to another room, that is, placed in isolation, that is, in solitary confinement. And not long after that, he was again taken from that room and did not come back, but he went through all those beatings right at the entrance as soon as he left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us Mr. Tulek's first name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Kemo. Kemo. Kemal or Kemo Tulek. His mother came from my village, so that I knew him a little, and it just happened that he was on duty in my village.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, Kemal Tulek is in Schedule C, number 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that he was brought back after the first rounds of beatings. Did you see -- first of all, what room was he kept in?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: He was in Room 22 and in my dormitory, because Room 22 had four subdivisions, but he was in my dormitory. We shared the same dormitory until he was taken away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when he was brought back from the beatings, could you see injuries on him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: No. When he returned from interrogation, no, he was not beaten then. It was as he left the solitary confinement where he was put temporarily, it was then, after that, that he was beaten and after that that he did not come back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said he was put in solitary confinement. Where specifically was he placed?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: It wasn't a proper isolation cell. It was a, it was a room on the same floor as our room was, to the right of the staircase and my room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if that room had a number?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if anybody was kept in that room with him, or was he completely by himself?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: He was all alone in that room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if there were people kept downstairs from that room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Downstairs from that room, beneath that room, were some Serb prisoners sentenced for various crimes, so two floors below were Serb prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw Kemal Tulek after he had been taken away for interrogation, did he tell you what had happened to him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: In not so many words, but as the guard waited for him in the door, he said that the interrogation -- they had accused him of being in possession of a weapon, and he claimed not to have ever had it. And that was all that he managed to tell us as he was leaving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you saw Kemal Tulek that time, did you see him again?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: No, never again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever interrogated?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Yes. Everybody had to go through interrogation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: It was one of those early days when we were brought there. I cannot remember the date. It was 1992, and they covered room by room, interrogating. It took some time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who conducted the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: I was interrogated by Zoran -- those were prewar investigators of the police, that is, MUP, MUP Foca, whom I knew before the war. Zoran Vladicic and Vojo Starovic, they were in the room. They were present in the room when I was interrogated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you mistreated during your interrogation?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: No. I was not, but my son, they also charged -- accused my son of having some explosive devices, put something on the table and said, "This was found in your house," and wanted to write the record, then you have to sign that record whether you like it or not. That was it. And as for me, no, they did not because I had an alibi which they believed, and that was at the time when the aggression began, I was at the construction site in Novi Sad with a Sarajevo company. And then I came to visit my family during a religious holiday, during Bajram, and I had to go through checkpoints and barricades, so that I simply found myself at the time of the aggression by my place, and they believed my story and did not ill-treat me, and I suppose that is how I survived the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that they charged or accused your son. Did they -- did he have a trial or a hearing on what they accused him of?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: No, there was no trial, but as he was coming back from the -- as he came back from the investigation, my son told me how they treated him and accused him of having been in possession of an explosive device and a weapon, but the lad never had anything. Nevertheless, he had to sign a statement to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were groups of detainees ever taken away and told they would be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Yes, there were such groups. All those groups which were taken away were told that they were about to be exchanged. "Get your things, you'll be exchanged." But the majority of those groups never turned up, although there were some smaller groups which were taken away to, say, our border, that is, to the border which was controlled by our army, and then they were released. That is how elderly men were taken away and then transferred to the territory under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any men from Jelec taken away and told they would be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Yes. The story was always the same when they took them away: "You will be exchanged."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many men from Jelec were taken out in this way?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Thirty-four, thirty-four of my neighbours were taken away and never returned, and a small number of them, as I said, those of a more advanced age, they survived. Thirty-four, and I have the list of all their first and last names. They were all my neighbours, or rather, my villagers, they were taken away and all trace of them is lost, and that group includes my son.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say all trace is lost, first, did you see them again at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you were released from KP Dom, did you ever see or hear from those 34 people?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: No, no one ever managed to get in touch from anywhere. We are all in contact. We are all from the same place, so all of us have been in touch until the present day. None of those 34 were ever heard from since.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said your son was among them. Could you tell us how you learned that your son had been taken away?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: My son was taken away on the 9th of September when mostly young men were taken out. At that -- on that day, I was on work duty within the so-called metal plant within this camp. On my way back from work around 3 p.m., I was told that my son was taken out for an exchange. I thought, well, let him be saved at least; however, that was only an illusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: I meant to say that I had hoped that he had been saved. Maybe that was my wish. Perhaps it was wrong for me to use this word "illusion." I mean my only wish was for my child to get out of there, even if I had to stay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you were released from KP Dom, did you make efforts to find your son?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Efforts were made to find him through the International Red Cross. This has been going on until the present day; however, there has been no trace whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned that you were on work duty at the metal workshop. Could you tell us how long you worked in the workshop?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: I joined in sometime in August, just before my son was taken away. Sometime in August I was taken there for work duty. All the way up to my release on the 10th of October, 1994, I was constantly involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you join that workforce voluntarily, or were you forced to?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: It looked voluntary. If you look at it, people were asking to leave these cells because they were starving. It seemed that we were all struggling for these jobs to work outside the compound. Nevertheless, this was forced labour. However, we all struggled on account of our Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. hunger because this gave people an extra meal, all of those who were in these work groups. However, I say that nevertheless this was forced labour. When people complained that they were sick or that they were injured and said that they could not go to the mines, for example, then there was no possibility for any absence, they simply had to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I'd like to have the witness shown Exhibit P6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned that one of the benefits of working was to be outside the compound. Could you show us where the metal workshop was located on this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. This is very small, so let me try to find my way. This is the main gate leading out of the prison compound. The next gate leads to the metal workshop. That is one of the workshops. This is Tokarija. Across opposite that one is the locksmith shop, and then is the mechanics shop. I worked in all three shops, depending on the work I actually did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you show us how you were taken to the workshop, what route you took.

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: We always had to pass by the main gate and to be checked there, then we got out of the prison compound, and then after a short time, to this gate that led to the metal shop compound. Every day except on Sundays.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On this diagram, if you look just above where the entrance building is, it looks like you can actually just walk through from the courtyards of the KP Dom into the workshop area. Was that possible, or was there some sort of barrier there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: There was no other entrance into the compound that was the workshop area. There must be some kind of mistake. There was a fence here, a wall. There is no such thing marked here. You couldn't pass through this at all. There was a wall there for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: If I could ask to have the ELMO light shut off. We no longer need the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kinds of things did you make in the metal shop?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Well, since the KP Dom was engaged in some kind of activity even before the war -- actually, they had a production process of their own. Before the war, they made furniture, and also the metal shop made various objects out of metal. They had a farm of their own outside Foca called Velecevo. As for the metal workshop, it involved the maintenance of vehicles, of the vehicles that belonged to them personally. They wanted to maintain the production of those metal kiosks for the market, so we continued making these metal kiosks, and I did that for a while. And then if there wasn't enough work to do, then I worked as a locksmith. And then if there wasn't enough to do there, then I went to help my colleague who worked as a mechanic on vehicle maintenance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever taken outside the workshop area to places in Foca itself to work?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Yes. I personally was taken out often, very often -- quite often outside the prison compound and outside the metal workshop area. I was taken to quite a few places in town to do various things. Of course, I was always escorted by prison guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken to work?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, I was taken to the city bakery where I worked on machine maintenance if something broke down. And then also the heating system of the city hospital, and then also the town school was -- the high school or was it the elementary school? It was this school in Aladza, at any rate, and it had the same kind of central heating system. Then also there was this farm in Velecevo, the maintenance of these farms, chicken farms, things like that. That's what we did. That's what I personally did. I forget to mention something else. There was a factory that made socks and stockings on the other side of the Drina, and that can be seen quite clearly from the camp. That is where this sock and stocking factory was where I also worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were taken out to these places to work, how did the townspeople treat you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: If we did not go far away from the camp, we didn't use a vehicle, we just went on foot in a column escorted by guards. There were some small provocations. People would say something. Sometimes some people would even run up to you and kick you or hit you with their hand, but that was about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the guards who were escorting you protect you from these provocations?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Well, in my view, if a prison guard would take me out of the prison compound, then he would be duty-bound to take me back, and therefore he would have to take care of me. But it's not that they really protected me. Sometimes, for example, they would answer these provocations. I remember once when one of the guards also said something provocative in response to yet another provocation. He said, "Why don't you catch yourself a Muslim, a Bosniak, and then do whatever you want with him."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in charge of the work duties?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Mr. Savo Todovic was in charge of the work duties. He's the one who carried out this selection, according to qualifications and skills, for various jobs. Often he would go into the prison compound; he would go to the various dormitories and make lists of various groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made a statement, Witness, to the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor on the 24th of June, 1996, regarding Savo Todovic, which I'd like you to explain. At page 5, you said: "He could force even sick persons to work. Nobody could overturn his decision." Could you explain what you meant by that last part, that nobody could overturn his decision?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Could anybody overturn that decision or not? I mean, we had no possibility of refusing to go to work once he had said so, because that would have only worsened our position, that is to say, our position within the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what Savo Todovic's formal position was, what his title was at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: I think that he was only in charge of us. I mean, as far as we, the inmates, are concerned, he was in charge only of these working groups that we were engaged in. In my opinion, this was a level lower than that of camp warden.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the camp warden while you were at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: In my opinion, it is an undeniable fact that Mr. Krnojelac was the camp warden from the time when I was brought in - that was June 1992 - until perhaps the end of 1993, when a certain Zoran came whom I did not know, nor did I remember his last name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know that Milorad Krnojelac was the camp warden?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: I could not have known during those first few days until I got out of the prison compound. Also when I worked further in the metal shop, I found out about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you find out? Who told you? Or did you conclude this from some other information?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: There was some information. I mean, during those 900 days, quite a bit of information had leaked. Quite a bit could be found out. What is most reliable is perhaps something that I am certain of, when the head of my metal shop entrusted me with a task of going to work on Mr. Krnojelac's house. He told me that I had to make three metal doors for the warden - that's what he said - within the metal workshop area. I made these metal doors, together with a colleague, and then I went to mount these three doors on Mr. Krnojelac's house, along with a group of construction workers who were involved in various other construction activities there, like on the roof, et cetera. Then also I made some metal stairs for the attic in that house, and also a metal skeleton for a bar that they had on the ground floor of that house that had burned down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned construction workers. Where were those construction workers taken from? Were they professionals?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: These were mainly construction workers from the prison compound. I really don't know, to tell you the truth, how well versed they were in these jobs. They were taking care of the roof and doing various other things. There were two of us locksmiths and a few other workers who were working on that house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many of you were taken from the KP Dom to work on Mr. Krnojelac's house?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: I just mentioned there were three metal workers, two locksmiths, and one general metal worker, and then three or four additional men who were working on the roof.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you taken to his house?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: We were taken by car only, the prison car -- actually, the van that belonged to the prison, and the prison guards drove us. On one occasion, Mitar Rasevic, who was commander of the guard, when he brought us to Mr. Krnojelac's house, Mitar Rasevic handed us over to Mr. Krnojelac's son. He was supposed to guard us while we worked there during the day and to finish our work. When we would finish our work at the end of the day, then the prison van would come back to pick us up and take us back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was Mr. Krnojelac's house located? In what neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: This was a neighbourhood in Foca called Donje Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you were -- those of you at the KP Dom were handed over to Krnojelac's son. Did Mr. Krnojelac's son have a job or did he function as a guard at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: No. During my stay at the KP Dom, I never saw him. I never saw him either in the prison compound or outside the prison compound or in the metal workshop area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While Mr. Krnojelac's son guarded you, did he wear any sort of uniform or carry any sort of weapon?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Yes. He had a camouflage uniform all the time and he only had a pistol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were at the Krnojelac house, did you meet any other members of the Krnojelac family?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion, his other son came in a wheelchair, and Mr. Krnojelac's wife, who brought us meals while we were working on his house. Also Mr. Krnojelac came while we were working.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of interaction did you have with Mr. Krnojelac himself?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Absolutely good, decent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say anything to you or the other detainees working there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Yes. There was conversation, exclusively related to the work we were doing; nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many -- what was the length of time that you worked on the Krnojelac house?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: I was there for three or four days, while the group that worked on the roof stayed a bit longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately what dates this was?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: The dates, I can't remember that, but I think it was the end of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Inside the KP Dom, did you ever see Mr. Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: He entered the prison compound very rarely, but he was often in the metal workshop area and also in front of the administration building. That's where he was very often. When we were going to and from work in the metal workshop area, we would see him there often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to clarify, when you say "in front of the administrative building," do you mean on the inside or the outside of the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: No. Completely outside the KP Dom. There were a few chairs there in front of the administration building. That's usually where they would sit there if the weather was nice. They would chat. We could notice that as we were passing by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just going back very briefly, because I forgot to ask you this before. When you said that -- when you worked on the Krnojelac house, was Mr. Krnojelac still the warden at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Well, as I said, this work was sometime in 1993. I can't remember the exact month. It was a long time ago. We did not dare write anything down. We would not dare keep any records when we went out or something like that, so I'm not sure whether he was still warden at that time or not. It might have been towards the end of his term.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did other detainees work? You mentioned a farm and you mentioned a mine. Perhaps we can get a little bit more detail on the mine. First of all, where was it located?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: The brown coal mine was about 15 kilometres away from Foca. It's a place called Miljevina. May I mention that, before the war, also the former prisoners of the KP Dom worked at the mine, so in order to keep production going at the mine, our inmates went there. A group went there every day except on Sundays. A vehicle took them there often, a KP Dom vehicle, and sometimes a vehicle of the Miljevina mine. But a prison guard would be there invariably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any detainees from Jelec work in the Miljevina mine?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear from people working there about what kind of work they did there and whether it was difficult?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Well, all work at a mine is difficult. They only worked on the extraction of ore in a primitive way, as the mine functioned before the war. Perhaps the conditions were even a bit more difficult. They didn't complain of anything in particular except for hunger and having enough stamina to go on, because this additional meal that they were given during working hours, they told us, was a can of 150 to 200 grammes of pate and also a quarter of a loaf of bread. After work, after they would get out of the pit, they would take a bath regularly before they went back to the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that when you went in and out of the KP Dom area, there was some sort of checkpoint. What were you checked for as you were going either out of or into, back into, the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: We were checked more as we came in. It all depended on the guard who would happen to be at that checkpoint. You had to take everything out of your pockets, and they would check everything that was being brought into the prison compound. Very often they took away food that sometimes these inmates would get, those who went out to work. For example, a person would pick an apple if he worked on the farm. Some guards would even take away an apple like that, or an extra slice of bread. They wouldn't allow them to bring it in. Whereas other guards would simply let you go in without any kind of check.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of the detainees who worked ever paid for the work they did?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: No, never. Had there been any adequate food, money, any remuneration, no way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The guards at the KP Dom, what kind of uniforms did they wear? Were they civilian or military?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: As regards uniforms, in the beginning you could see all sorts. Some wore prewar dark blue uniforms, others had been mobilised to the compound and wore the uniforms of the former Yugoslav army, and the majority also had camouflage uniforms. But in the early days they came in all shapes and sizes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on in your stay at the KP Dom, did there -- did the uniforms change?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Yes. In 1994, standard uniforms were designed for those prison guards, and they were, yes, of different colours; camouflage, but dark blue and black. They were mostly camouflage uniforms and they were designed for the prison staff mostly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see guards going to the front line?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Yes. They took shifts during mobilisation. They went group by group, would go for a fortnight and come back, and took shifts that way, but I believe that everybody had to go through it, except the highest-placed officials in the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whom would you count among those people?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Well, I mean the warden of the KP Dom, Todovic, and Mitar Rasevic, guard commander, they were always there and they only dealt with the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said "the warden," could you tell us who you meant?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: What I always say is that it is an irrefutable fact that Mr. Krnojelac was the warden, but whether he had a say and how much weight he could pull in the compound, I do not know. I do not know if he would change anything or help, perhaps, or help the prisoners. Or how much he actually took part in crimes, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you finally released from KP Dom? What was the date?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: The 10th of October, 1994, through the good offices of the International Committee of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether it was a military exchange or purely a civilian one?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: It was a civilian exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of your exchange, did you have any contact or did you see any military commanders in Miljevina?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: We had some trouble with the exchange because it failed that first day, or rather, at that first moment. From Foca to Sarajevo we were taken in a car, escorted by prison authorities and the military, and we were brought to Sarajevo, to another camp called Kula. But when we entered Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that other compound, that some complications, some problems arose, I don't know what they were, so that we were never -- we never got off that bus. And some guys in camouflage uniforms ran out and threatened the driver and escort and everybody and told us that we were to go back to Foca. So the bus went back to Miljevina. So slightly before Foca, we stopped there at a -- by a motel, and that motel served as a kind of a headquarters or something for the Serb army, and we stayed there for about half an hour. They tried to talk to somebody, seek somebody's advice. They allowed us to get off the bus for a short while to relieve ourselves and things like that. So there were some consultations and discussion, and as far as we could understand, they were talking to Mr. Kovac. And evidently that agreement yielded fruit so that we did not go back to Foca and, instead, went back to that camp in Sarajevo, Kula, and that is when the exchange went through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what position that Mr. Kovac had?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Well, from what we could hear, he was a commander. He was the commander of a unit. I couldn't say which formation, battalion, or something of the Foca Corps that he was the Commander-in-Chief, because we could hear quite often when they would announce the mobilisation over a car equipped with the PA system, and that mobilisation would be signed by somebody called Kovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the whole time that you were kept at KP Dom, the 900 or so days that you described, were you ever told why you were being kept there and for so long?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: There was no explanation. Every day we spent there was full of uncertainty. Nobody communicated with us until the Red Cross came and registered the inmates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when were you registered?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Well, the Red Cross made it through only on the 23rd of June, 1993, which is more than a year after I was brought to the KP Dom. That was the first time that the International Red Cross came, even though they tried to do so before that but were not allowed to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to when you were working at Mr. Krnojelac's house and you saw one of his sons in a wheelchair. Did you ever do any work for that son?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: On yet another occasion, as the chief of the metal shop told me, I had to do a metal, a metal rack for the office of the warden's son because he was given this outlet in the centre of Foca. And I did it in the metal shop, those racks, those shelves, but I didn't go to mount them in that outlet, even though I did go there once in order to take measurements, of course, in order to make all those shelves and racks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that it was that son rather than the other son, the one who was not in a wheelchair, that this is the work you were doing?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: I think that that business premises were given to his son because he lost his extremities in the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a result of your detention in the KP Dom, can you tell us how you suffered physically?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: I didn't suffer any physical consequences except fear and hunger. I was not beaten or anything. I was very lucky. I was one of the few who were never beaten. So that except for everyday fear that I might be liquidated and the fact that I was starved, that I was famished, nothing else. But these, of course, are lasting consequences.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Cross-examination, Mr. Vasic. Cross-examined by Mr. Vasic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To begin with, good afternoon. I'm Miroslav Vasic, and I'm one of the counsel for the accused Milorad Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if there were any crisis staffs in Foca before the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: I believe there were some Crisis Staffs, both in your army and in our army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And was there Crisis Staff in Jelec, too?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Yes, there was one in Jelec.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this Crisis Staff, was it responsible for the defence of Jelec?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Well, you could say that. The protection of Jelec insofar as it was possible to protect it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. How many statements did you make to the OTP investigators, could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: I gave one statement. Now, was it 1998 in Sarajevo? I gave one statement -- or, rather, it took two days, really. I gave it, but it was one statement because I didn't finish the first day, so we went on the second day, but it was one statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it on the 14th and the 24th of June, 1996?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Believe me, I can't remember the date, but it was Sarajevo when I gave the statement, and the date, I really don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just hold it. You are starting your questions while the translation is still well and truly underway, Mr. Vasic. And for the witness's sake, do pause after you've heard the question finish before you begin your answer. That is because the one translator has to take both the question and the answer and they have to catch up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to ask the usher to help me show you a copy of your statement that we were given by the OTP. One is in Bosnian and the other one in English, and you will tell us if that is the statement that you mentioned that you gave to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it is 274 and 274A. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps it will be better if you looked at the English version because it has your signature, if that is your signature.

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. It is my signature. 24th of June, 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Usher, could you please return those statements back to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give any other statements after this statement, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you on the 25th of September, 1998, perhaps, give another statement, or would it be easier for you if I showed you copies of that statement, too?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Well, let me see.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will the usher please help me once again. These have numbers. The numbers are 275 and 275A.

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature, 1998. I've just mentioned 1998, but 1996 I omitted. I forgot it. I knew about this one, of 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the copies back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified today that you arrived in KP Dom on the 1st of June, 1992. Could you tell us if you heard from other prisoners whether before you came to the KP Dom there was in it ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the counsel's microphone is turned off. I could not hear the end of the question.

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Yes, I heard it from the men who were in the camp before me, or rather, those who came to the camp before me, that there were the troops of the so-called Uzice Corps whom I did not find there when I got there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, you turned your microphone off before you finished asking your last question. Are you able to reconstruct what the question was?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. Thank you, Your Honours. My question was whether, after he came to the KP Dom, he heard from other prisoners whether there had been any military troops in the KP Dom before he came there, before he got there.

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Do you want me to answer again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, thank you. Your answer came out very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me how long did those troops stay in KP Dom, according to them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: I don't know. I did not find them there, and I wouldn't be able to tell you how long they were there, when they arrived, because I just don't know. But be that as it may, I did not find them there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, in your statement to the OTP, in the statement of the 24th and 25th of -- the 14th and 24th of June, 1996, did you state there that the troops of the Uzice Corps had access to the prison for several early days of the war before you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: No, I could not say that. I could not say how long they were there. But the beginning of the aggression against Foca, I believe it started in May, or rather April, May - I wouldn't know the date - until that day, until the liberation of Foca. I believe they were there until that day, but I wouldn't know. So it's April, May, and then we come to June, so it's a couple of months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So until June?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Well, I didn't find them there, so they must have left before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. When you came to the KP Dom, could you tell us: What did the guards wear, the majority of them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: I told you, there were all kinds of uniforms, but those guards who were also the guards before the war in the KP Dom in Foca, they were mostly in those professional uniforms, which were dark blue. And while -- and there were also some in camouflage uniforms and uniforms of the former army, the Yugoslav one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see guards go to the front?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I did not see them go, but I could see them get ready for it in front of the administrative building, in full combat gear, and there would be a military vehicle waiting for them, the vehicle of the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In front of the KP Dom, did you see military vehicles and equipment?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Quite often. They would even come into the compound, to the metal shop where I worked. I remember once a car belonging to Bosnian Serbs entered with a mounted anti-aircraft gun, mounted on that vehicle, and we had to strengthen it, to fix it better to the floor of that military vehicle. They must have been preparing it for the front. And this is a fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You told us that you were assigned to the metal workshop and that there you used to see Mr. Krnojelac. And did you tell the OTP investigators in 1998 the following? It is ID 275A in our language and it says: "As I worked in the metal workshop -- when I worked in the metal workshop, he would come to pay us a visit," meaning Mr. Krnojelac. "He would only greet us but would not talk to us. He treated us correctly. He was quite decent with us. One could not see that he hated us. He did not insult us, nor did he speak against Muslims." Did you say this to OTP investigators?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Yes, that is absolutely correct. I can repeat it today, that he is guilty because he served wrong, because he accepted that office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Members of the Krnojelac family - and you told us that you met them when you worked on his house - how did they behave? How did they treat you and other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: They were correct, absolutely; one could even say friendly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet Mr. Krnojelac's wife?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Yes, and I was very favourably impressed. I thought she was a good woman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, sir: Did she bring you food regularly, to the house, I mean, where you worked?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Yes. Meals were regular, they were good, the quantities were sufficient, and it was served in a friendly way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke today about how prisoners were taken for beatings. Could you tell us if it only happened at night?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Yes, only at night, or rather early evening hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell OTP investigators how, after a guard would arrive with a list and take a person away, how he would take that person to a door leading out of the compound and that, after that, that person would be presumably given over to the military police?

utterances.speaker: FWS-144
utterances.text: Yes, because this mention of the military police and why we thought about -- why it occurred to us was during the interrogation of prisoners, because those investigators threatened us. They tried to force us to own up to certain acts which they tried to attribute to us, or else they would turn us over to the military police. So that is why we assumed that these people were being taken over by military authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, you have some time to go, have you, in your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honour. I do have some questions, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I understand that, but one of us has an appointment which I think, if we can adjourn a few minutes early, it would be easier for the Judge to attend that appointment. So we'll adjourn now until Monday at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: be reconvened on Monday, the 29th day of January, 2001, at 9.30 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
